sources.title: White House says the US is lifting tariffs on some Canadian goods

discussion.body: If the relief is paired with higher levies elsewhere, the aggregate tariff burden may barely move, and the headline is doing most of the work.
Aggregates don't import anything. For the firm buying packing crates or refrigeration equipment, 30 October is the only number in the story that matters.
Fair — and the White House's own framing, prosperity and national security, tells you the list is meant to be a lever rather than a ledger.

items.title: Washington Swaps Plywood for Valves on Its Canadian Tariff List
items.body:
The US is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods, with the White House saying on Friday that it was working to protect the economic prosperity and national security of the American people. According to a White House statement, from 30 October certain products come off the list of Canadian goods the US taxes: plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and certain packing crates and boxes.

The same statement added that those items would be replaced with certain valves, carpets and waste products, among others. The Wall Street Journal reported that the reductions could be offset by raising levies on other Canadian goods. Read the two lists side by side and this looks less like a rollback than a reshuffle: specific line items out, specific line items in, all dated to the last day of the month.

sources.title: Ancient Rome: A City of Immigrants

discussion.body: The fault line here isn't numbers at all. A city can be overwhelmingly composed of newcomers and their children and still have thin institutions binding them to one another.
An immigrant neighborhood is exactly where the weak-ties verdict should strain: clustering in one district is hard to square with foreigners whose connections were mostly ephemeral.

Careful, though — what we would now call an immigrant neighborhood is a modern label fitted onto an ancient district. It tells us about clustering; it doesn't tell us how the residents thought about themselves.

items.title: Rome at Its Height: Perhaps a Million People, Most of Them Immigrants or Their Descendants
items.body:
Historian Ryan R. Abrecht calls ancient Rome a city of immigrants: a pre-modern metropolis of perhaps a million people at its height, most of them immigrants or the descendants of immigrants.

Modern historians overwhelmingly agree that immigration profoundly shaped Rome's demographics and history. What they have argued over is community: some have held that there was little sense of immigrant community at Rome at all.

At the scale of a single district the picture sharpens. By the first century CE, the Roman district beyond the Tiber had become what we would now call an immigrant neighborhood — a veritable Little Middle East. That is a claim about streets, not about the whole city, which is what makes it useful against a verdict delivered at citywide scale.

sources.title: RFK Jr.’s vaccine injury clinic could damage NIH hospital, board warns

discussion.body: The provocation was a stunt: a surprise ribbon-cutting at the hospital for Kennedy's signature vaccine injury clinic. That makes the objection institutional rather than abstract.

Leslie's caveat complicates the rebuke: he has no concerns about studying potential vaccine injuries, and he calls serious reactions rare but real. That is a different position from dismissing vaccine-injury research outright.

items.title: Oversight board chair rebukes Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy over anti-vaccine activities
items.body:
At a meeting of the board that oversees the National Institutes of Health's Clinical Center Research Hospital, chair Jack Leslie diverted from the agenda and spent six minutes delivering a pointed rebuke of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, warning that Kennedy's anti-vaccine activities could tarnish the hospital, often called the “house of hope” for patients with rare conditions or those who have exhausted other options.

Leslie also said he has no concerns about studying potential injuries from vaccines.

sources.title: Same scam. 2 countries. Why Canadians don’t get their money back

discussion.body: The case for shifting responsibility is an information-asymmetry argument: the bank is better able to identify and stop scams than the customer.
But that advantage has a shadow: scammers borrow the bank's authority. One caller posed as Tangerine's fraud department and told the customer his card had to be collected as evidence.

items.title: Why Britain's Scam Rules Put the Bank in the Detection Seat
items.body:
Two people described the same financial scam to police and banks; the only difference was where they lived—one in Canada, the other in the U.K.

Andrei Skorobogatov, a strategic advisor of Britain's regulations, says shifting the burden of responsibility from customer to bank is a recognition that financial institutions are better able to identify and stop scams.

He argues that the public going about day-to-day business will probably struggle to detect a scam, while a bank with highly sophisticated detection mechanisms is in a much better place to do so.

sources.title: Apocalypse Troy: Nolan’s Odyssey and the End of Civilization

discussion.body: The reveal makes hospitality the load-bearing rule: it is a breach of xenia that dissolves the entire logic of civilization.
The detail about future generations having only songs makes the apocalypse a memory problem too: what remains is a story, not a world.

items.title: Nolan's Odyssey Turns the Sack of Troy Into an Apocalypse
items.body:
Christopher Nolan's Odyssey does not declare itself post-apocalyptic until the very end.

The twist is that the sack of Troy was such a violent breach of Zeus' law of xenia—hospitality—that it dissolved the entire logic of civilization.

The Age of Bronze is doomed, and later generations will have only songs to remember its makers.

sources.title: Everybody panic: A Valve developer said "HLX" in public

discussion.body: A code name that has sat in engine code since at least 2024 and never been said in public until now is the most Valve possible form of communication.
A code name is a label, not a shipping date. The interesting question is what Valve does with the label next.

items.title: A Valve Composer Let 'HLX' Slip During an Audio Panel
items.body:
At a panel on Valve's use of open audio engines, Valve composer and audio artist Mike Morasky was discussing high dynamic range audio when he said that HLX has its own version.

According to Ars Technica, HLX is widely reported to be the internal code name for Valve's next Half-Life project; the label has appeared in Valve engine code since at least 2024.

Ars Technica says no Valve employee had referenced the codename in public until this panel, though Morasky had a close call in an interview last year. That makes the remark a mention, not a trailer.

sources.title: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide

discussion.body: The line item that should worry agent builders is the train dimension. It is the largest of the three in this run and it grows with the length of the trajectory, so a chatty agent is an expensive agent.

A lower per-token price helps, and AWS chose GPT-OSS-20B partly because its reasoning effort is controllable per request. But the train dimension still scales with trajectory length, so the bigger lever is getting the agent to stop explaining itself.

items.title: In an AWS Training Run, the Train Tokens Ate the Budget
items.body:
An agent that files an expense report or triages a support ticket takes a sequence of actions, and each step depends on what came before.

AWS's MTRL service is serverless: you pick a base model and it provisions the training and sampling infrastructure. You pay per million tokens in three dimensions, priced by base model.

In its 100-step run, AWS reports 491.6 million prefill tokens, 159.7 million sample tokens, and 643.3 million train tokens across 105,486 rollouts in 12 hours 40 minutes. At GPT-OSS-20B list prices in US East (N. Virginia) at the time of writing, that comes to about $339. The train dimension dominates and scales with trajectory length, so shorter games and less verbose reasoning cut the bill; in this setup, an agent's verbosity is a line item.

sources.title: Fish Addiction: An Ancient Greek Paranoia

discussion.body: Ioannis M. Konstantakos writes that Philoxenus caused his own death by devouring a gigantic octopus; the deathbed scene has the doctor called, his affairs in order, his life's work complete, and one last wish—to finish the final bite of octopus and take it with him to the Underworld.
Calling that resignation is generous. The man is packing a snack for the afterlife.

items.title: Opsophagos: A Fish Addict, and an Athenian Comic Type
items.body: According to legend, the ancient Greek poet Philoxenus wished for a throat as long as a crane's so he could stretch out the time he spent swallowing. An opsophagos is a fish addict—someone whose desire for seafood becomes a self-destructive obsession. The root of the word is opson, which originally referred to anything that might accompany a starchy, grain-based staple but came more and more to signify fish. In memory, Philoxenus became a stock character out of Athenian comedy: the opsophagos.

sources.title: NASA, Virginia Launch Power Partnership for Energy Security

discussion.body: The concrete mechanism is a digital pipeline: Virginia Energy can connect to Langley's POWER platform, download specific datasets, and put them directly into its modeling tools.

The outcomes are still promises: NASA says the partnership will help Virginians better anticipate energy demand, prepare for extreme weather, and understand factors affecting electricity generation, supporting a more reliable and resilient system. That is a promissory note, not a result.

items.title: NASA Will Supply Weather and Solar Data for Virginia's Energy Planning
items.body:
NASA and Virginia Energy have a new Space Act Agreement, announced at a Friday ceremony, to use NASA atmospheric-science expertise for resiliency studies, resource analysis, and long-term energy planning. The partnership is between NASA's Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia, and the Virginia Department of Energy; it is meant to support decisions on energy generation, delivery, and use by providing solar, meteorological, and future weather-risk datasets for energy-system modeling and planning.

NASA says the agreement will help state officials plan for current and potential extreme weather in Virginia and assess implications for electricity demand, energy generation, and system stress.

sources.title: Ohio could decide control of the Senate. Its rural voters might decide the winner

discussion.body: The week-or-two test is unfair as a policy audit but useful as a political one: it asks whether officials can recognize the arithmetic of a grocery bill.
Recognizing the arithmetic is not the same as knowing what to do about it. A complaint at a market is a mood, not a manifesto.

items.title: A 62-year-old Athens resident's challenge to politicians: live like me for a week or two
items.body:
At the farmers market, a 62-year-old lifelong Athens resident told NPR that gas, utilities and groceries have become burdensome.

He said he wished politicians could spend 'a week or two living like I do.'

Ohio is now considered reliably Republican, but this election is a little different.

sources.title: Freed US citizen was tortured in Russian jail, former Ukrainian prisoners say

discussion.body: Two prisoners' accounts lining up with the family's statements is the kind of corroboration that gives a torture allegation weight.
Weight for the record, maybe. For politics, the release coming on the day Witkoff met Putin is suggestive without proving a bargain.

items.title: Fellow prisoners describe beatings of freed American Stephen Hubbard
items.body:
Ukrainians held alongside Stephen Hubbard have said they witnessed him being beaten and humiliated by Russian guards, the BBC reports. Shyshko said he witnessed and heard Hubbard being beaten by prison guards and electrocuted with a stun gun.

Shyshko, a captured Ukrainian soldier, alleges Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of prison staff. Accounts from the two former Ukrainian prisoners corroborate statements made by Hubbard's family that he was tortured in prison.

The 74-year-old was released by the Kremlin after four-and-a-half years, on the day US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg to discuss the war in Ukraine.

sources.title: Pedro Pascal on Learning Cello for ‘Behemoth!,’ Why ‘You’ve Got to Eat S—’ to Make It in Hollywood and the ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Line His Character Says

discussion.body: “A highly intense lip sync” is a wonderfully unromantic way to describe months of practice: the illusion was the work, and by his account the work was the hardest thing he had ever done.
The lip sync is the funniest detail, but the bet made before the greenlight is the real one — lessons for a film that might never have been made.

items.title: Pedro Pascal Took Cello Lessons for a Film That Hadn't Been Greenlit
items.body:
Pedro Pascal's own verdict on his cello playing is blunt: “If you could hear it, you would think I was killing an animal.”

He had been at it for more than a year, having started lessons for a movie that had not been greenlit yet.

That movie is Behemoth!, and Variety reports Pascal first had lunch with Tony Gilroy in late July 2025 about taking on the lead role in Gilroy's latest film.

sources.title: Developer wants to build 500 modular homes on roof of struggling Sask. mall

discussion.body: Measuring your housing project against three million pounds of cars and light trucks is a genuinely charming piece of advocacy: the engineering claim is boring in the best way, which is probably why he leads with it.

Weight answers one question. Scott Bell, a geography and planning professor, says he has not seen a project that puts housing on top of an existing structure, and Alrifai is still preparing the formal plans for the city — a warm reception from staff is not a yes.

items.title: A Saskatchewan Mall's Roof Is the Proposed Site for 500 Modular Homes
items.body:
Alrifai's firm bought the Gateway Mall in Prince Albert, Sask., earlier this year and has announced plans to build 500 modular housing units on its roof, replacing a parking lot. In Alrifai's framing, a struggling mall in central Saskatchewan has a future that comes down to arithmetic.

Louai Alrifai, whose firm bought the mall, puts the case for the roof this way: “700 cars and light trucks weigh around 3,000,000 pounds. Our modules weigh much less.”

The company says each unit will cover 329 square feet and rent for $1,000 a month.

sources.title: Rabelais’ Ancient Greek: An Epigram of 1524

discussion.body: Choosing Greek over Latin at a moment when Greek’s standing in France was precarious is the real content of the gesture: a claim about which readers you want to be counted among, made in a language the establishment distrusted.

Or the gesture is social rather than defiant. The poem is a dedication in a book by André Tiraqueau, the humanist and jurist based in Poitou who was Rabelais’ patron and close acquaintance — a gift to a friend, not a manifesto.

The joke is that the poem need not be good for either reading to hold: it is an occasional short piece, by no means outstanding in its own right, whose value is as a witness to Greek’s growing place in French letters and to Rabelais’ own ambitions. The gesture matters more than the verse.

items.title: Rabelais Wrote a Greek Epigram While Greek’s Place in France Was Precarious
items.body:
Rabelais’ oeuvre includes one independent poetic composition in Greek: a short epigram that survives as one of the earliest pieces of Greek composition from early-modern France. It appears as a dedication in the third edition of De Legibus Connubialibus, André Tiraqueau’s treatise on marital law and women’s legal capacity, first published in 1513.

The interesting choice is the language. Rabelais chose Greek over Latin at a time when Greek’s position in France was still precarious, and humanist efforts to strengthen it, his own included, met resistance from ecclesiastical authorities.

sources.title: The Sopranos begets the cult of Don't Stop Believin'

discussion.body: The 'or you're done, dude' is the best part. Strip it away and you have a fridge magnet; keep it and you have a father telling a struggling musician to get real while also telling him not to quit.
But the song was already a huge US hit in 1981. The Sopranos didn't rescue an obscure track; it gave a familiar one a second life.

items.title: A father's warning became a chorus in 'Don't Stop Believin''; a Sopranos final scene gave it a new generation.
items.body:
Jonathan Cain's father gave him the words 'don't stop believin'. He ended every phone call to his son, a struggling musician in Los Angeles, with: 'Don't stop believing or you're done, dude.' When Cain joined Journey in 1980, he had worked the phrase into a chorus, and his new bandmates developed it into a song.

The song was a huge US hit in 1981, but 26 years later it found a new audience when it appeared in the final scene of The Sopranos. An early Glee episode then helped make it unstoppable.

sources.title: Reinforcing the value of human understanding at MIT

discussion.body: The careful wording is 'not ... alone.' Practical application stays on the scale; the argument is only that something else belongs there too. That is a more defensible position than treating usefulness as irrelevant.

Yet Rayo himself says SHASS research helps address climate change and AI. If that isn't practical application, the word is doing strange work. The distinction may be less between useful and useless than between different kinds of use.

items.title: MIT's humanities, arts and social sciences dean says practical use isn't the only measure
items.body:
At the MIT School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences' 75th Anniversary Symposium, speakers explored how artificial intelligence is transforming teaching, research, and society. Agustín Rayo, the Kenan Sahin Dean of SHASS and a professor of philosophy, said that while the school's research addresses global issues such as climate change and AI, its value should not be measured by practical application alone.

Education, he said, should also help us ask what is worth doing, what we owe one another, and what makes a life worth living. Some research matters because it helps us understand the histories, cultures, and social structures that have made us who we are.

sources.title: A D.C. park was made 'for the pleasure of the people.' Trump's plan would change that

discussion.body: Race organizers are already looking into backup options for next year given the rumored renovations, event director Rob Wolfe told NPR. Wolfe also said the park's future matters more than the race's Sunday in April or the Marine Corps Marathon's Sunday in October. That is a gracious thing for an event director to say when his own race is the thing at risk.

The trees are the harder fact to swallow: the government downed hundreds of them on the course with little warning earlier this month, and critics worry it was a pretext for starting the renovations. The government says it was following up on recommendations from a 2019 landscaping report. A report explains the reason for cutting; it does not make the timing feel less odd.

items.title: Trump Says the Renovation Would Close a D.C. Park for 15 Months
items.body:
Trump's stated wish to take over the East Potomac Golf Links thrust a municipal D.C. golf course into the national spotlight. Locals rely on the area for much more than golf and worry the district could lose a recreational oasis.

On Truth Social, Trump said renovations would keep the entire park closed for 15 months starting in November. It is not clear what would be left when it reopens: the rendering he posted shows an 18-hole course spanning the entire peninsula, including the current playground and picnic area on its southern tip, with no road visible around the perimeter.

sources.title: El Gouna’s CineGouna Expands Industry Push: ‘We Want to Give Every Filmmaker a Chance’

discussion.body: The volatility may matter more than the size of any single cheque. Regional funds have helped fill part of the gap, but Shawky says their resources can fluctuate, leaving filmmakers unsure what support is available. Uncertainty deserves its own line in the budget.
The other shortage is people: Amer argues that funding is certainly an issue, but that creative producers are badly needed. A cheque is easy to count; producing judgment is not.

items.title: CineGouna's Funding Chief Says Egypt Has 100 Years of Cinema and No National Film Fund
items.body:
At El Gouna this week, CineGouna Funding awarded more than $350,000 in cash and services, with 40 awards going to 16 of the 19 participating projects.

Ahmed Shawky, who heads the fund, describes three gaps in the Arab world: many countries have no national film funds, co-production treaties are limited, and regional funding is volatile.

Egypt is his example. Shawky, a film critic and festival programmer, says the country's film commission focuses on attracting foreign productions rather than financing local films, and that Egypt has no national film fund despite 100 years of cinema history and more than 4,000 features.

sources.title: Police officer who shot and killed 1-year-old boy in Mississippi has resigned, mayor says

discussion.body: The official finding is the part that matters: the attorney general's monthslong probe concluded the force was justified.
That finding is contested. Ben Crump says the footage shows the fatal shot came from the side of the car, disputing that Foster was in imminent danger.

items.title: A Mississippi Officer Who Shot and Killed a 1-Year-Old Resigned. The Attorney General's Office Had Cleared Him.
items.body:
A Mississippi police officer who shot and killed a 1-year-old boy while firing into a moving vehicle while responding to a shoplifting call has resigned, the mayor of Senatobia told the Associated Press.

Sgt. Hunter Foster, 33, had been cleared of criminal wrongdoing earlier in the week; the Mississippi attorney general's office concluded after a monthslong probe that his use of force was justified.

Ben Crump, an attorney for the family, said footage of the shooting shows the fatal shot came from the side of the car, disputing that Foster was in imminent danger.

sources.title: How to live a life of awe

discussion.body: Awe is defined by vastness and mystery, not by a destination; Keltner's point is that the mountain is optional.
Optional, yes, but if awe is a human universal rooted in evolutionary history, the everyday version may be a quieter thing than the definition's 'beyond comprehension' suggests.

items.title: You Don't Need Kilimanjaro to Feel Awe
items.body:
Awe is the feeling of stepping out of the ordinary and encountering something vast, mysterious and beyond your comprehension.

Psyche describes it as a human universal, rooted in our evolutionary history to make us feel connected to the world beyond us.

Dacher Keltner, a psychologist at UC Berkeley, argues in a Psyche video that you don't need to summit Mount Kilimanjaro or see the Northern Lights to get its rewards.
